rejected.title: Voice across poetry, novels and film
card: Each form of text gives a writer different tools for building voice. To study voice, look at the tools that form has.
Poetry
voice often comes through rhythm, line breaks and sound. A short, broken rhythm can make a speaker sound anxious.
Novel
voice often comes through narration. A first-person narrator shares private thoughts in their own words, so readers hear their personality.
Film
voice can come through voice-over, where a character speaks over the images. The speaker's tone, along with what we see on screen, shapes how we feel.
rejected.remember: Voice is built with the tools each form offers, so ask how this form works.

a.q: Which technique most directly builds a speaker's voice in a poem?
opts: Camera shots that follow the speaker
a.why: Poems often build voice through rhythm, line breaks and sound. Voice-over and camera shots belong to film, and chapters of narration belong to novels.
a.clue: Which tool belongs to poetry, not film or novels?

b.q: In Jai's film, an old fisher speaks in a slow, gruff tone over shots of an empty harbour, telling us what he regrets. Which technique is building his voice?
b.why: The fisher speaks over the images, which is voice-over. His slow tone might suggest rhythm, but rhythm and line breaks are poetry tools, and chapters and stanzas belong to written forms.
b.clue: He speaks over the pictures on screen.

a.q: In a poem, which technique most directly builds the speaker's voice?
opts: Camera shots that follow the speaker
a.why: Poems often build voice through rhythm, line breaks and sound. Voice-over and camera shots belong to film, and chapters of first-person narration belong to novels.
a.clue: Which tool belongs to poetry rather than to film or novels?

b.q: Jai's short film shows an empty harbour at dawn. We never see the old fisher, but we hear him, slow and gruff, telling us what he regrets. Which technique is building his voice?
b.why: We hear the fisher while the screen shows the empty harbour, so the film uses voice-over, and his slow, gruff tone shapes how we feel about him. Close-ups are tempting because they are a film tool, but we never see his face. Line breaks belong to poetry and chapter narration to novels, so neither is building his voice here.
b.clue: How do we come to know the fisher if he never appears on screen?
